clue.text: Graduates's research station returns the ointment

indicators.note: something that returns comes back the way it went, so the words before are read from right to left

blocks.note: a Master of Arts is a graduate
the possessive ending taken as written
short for laboratory

explanation.surface: A graduate's research laboratory sends back the ointment it was testing.
explanation.walkthrough: The graduate's lab, MA'S LAB, is read backwards as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Balsam is an aromatic resin used as a soothing healing salve or balm.

clue.text: Notice the formal letter allowing entry

blocks.note: an advertisement, a notice in a paper
a missive is a formal or official letter

explanation.surface: Someone spots an official letter granting them admission.
explanation.definitionFit: Admissive is a rare adjective describing something that admits or permits, so it lets things in.

clue.text: Half county's transport one dismissed as a financial burden ...

indicators.note: half means only the first part of the county's name is kept
something dismissed is sent away, so a letter leaves the word

blocks.note: the first half of Surrey, a county south of London
a taxi with one, I, taken away
I as the Roman numeral, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A county's transport worker is sacked, a heavy cost to bear.
explanation.walkthrough: TAXI loses its I (one) to leave TAX.
explanation.definitionFit: A surtax is an additional levy on top of normal taxation, an extra monetary load.

clue.text: ...  one tramload could be awkward ...

indicators.note: could be suggests a possible alternative arrangement of the letters given

blocks.note: I as the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the transport story, a single full tram might prove clumsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Maladroit is a French-derived word for clumsy or inept, lacking skill or grace.

clue.text: What one goes back to at the drawing-board?

definitions.text: What one goes back to at the drawing-board?

blocks.clueFragment: What one goes back to at the drawing-board?
blocks.note: surface: what a designer returns to when starting a plan again
setter's reading: the idiom of going back to fundamentals, as in starting from scratch

explanation.walkthrough: Going back to the drawing-board and going back to the fundamentals are both idioms for starting over.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase back to basics means returning to simple essential principles, just like restarting a design.

clue.text: ...  and no transport turns up for painter

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the words are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a cab is a taxi

explanation.surface: Ending the transport saga: no vehicle arrives to collect the artist.
explanation.walkthrough: NO CAB is read upwards. Francis Bacon was a twentieth-century British painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon was an Irish-born British artist famous for disturbing figurative canvases, so he is an example.

clue.text: Function? To preserve a cushy job!

blocks.note: sine is a trigonometric function
to cure meat or fish is to preserve it

explanation.surface: Someone asks what an office is for: merely keeping an easy post.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinecure is a paid position requiring little or no work, the classic easy number.

clue.text: The town's team, they say

indicators.note: they say points to how the word is spoken rather than how it is written

blocks.note: a crew is a team of rowers or workers

explanation.surface: People talk about the local town's sports side.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is'. Crewe is a railway town in Cheshire, north-west England, pronounced just like crew.
explanation.definitionFit: Crewe is an English railway junction settlement in Cheshire, so it is an example place.

clue.text: Old transport for the chop?

blocks.note: surface: an outdated vehicle destined for the scrapheap
setter's reading: literally heading to the guillotine, the cart that carried the condemned in revolutionary France

explanation.walkthrough: Being for the chop usually means about to be scrapped; here it is the blade itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbrel was a two-wheeled cart used to carry prisoners to execution during the French Revolution.

clue.text: Work without security on locks for sirens

blocks.note: a temp works short-term with no job security
locks and tresses are both long hair

explanation.surface: Agency staff do the hair of seductive women.
explanation.definitionFit: Sirens are alluring, seductive women, named after the mythical singers who lured sailors to wreck.

clue.text: Fight continued to the finish

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for continued
the end is the finish

explanation.surface: A battle carried on until one side was finished.
explanation.definitionFit: To contend is to struggle or compete against an opponent, a verb meaning battle.

clue.text: Centre minds to settle for good judgement

indicators.note: letters left to settle find a new, rearranged order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Calm your thoughts so that you can decide wisely.
explanation.definitionFit: Discernment is the ability to perceive and decide well, keen insight in assessing things.

clue.text: Young sprouts in the salad?

blocks.note: surface: perhaps children, young sprogs, playing in a salad bowl
setter's reading: literally seedlings, the paired sprouting greens grown on damp tissue and eaten young

explanation.walkthrough: Sprouts sounds like Brussels sprouts or slang for children; it means seedling shoots.
explanation.definitionFit: The two seedling crops are grown together and harvested within days as a garnish for sandwiches and salads.

clue.text: Make ready for sailing while in dock

blocks.note: first meaning: to adjust the sails and balance of a boat
second meaning: to cut short, as a tail is docked

explanation.surface: A crew gets the boat ready while it is still moored.
explanation.walkthrough: Dock looks like a harbour; it is the verb for cutting short.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors adjust sails and ballast to get a vessel shipshape, and the same verb means clip or cut back.

clue.text: Indecisive boundary row

blocks.note: a border is a boundary
a row is a line

explanation.surface: An argument over where a frontier lies goes unsettled.
explanation.walkthrough: Row looks like a quarrel; it is a straight line.
explanation.definitionFit: A borderline case sits on the margin between categories, so it is uncertain and not clear-cut.

clue.text: Man in defiance is becoming more obscure

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other

blocks.note: daring is boldness, defiance of danger
a man's name

explanation.surface: A defiant man is growing harder to understand.
explanation.definitionFit: Darkening means growing dimmer or less clear, so things gradually turn murkier and harder to see.

clue.text: Perform mathematical task and get in tangle with estimate

indicators.note: a tangle is a muddle, so the letters beside it are knotted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
to rate is to estimate or assess

explanation.surface: A student muddles a calculus problem while trying to estimate the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To integrate is the calculus operation of finding an integral, a standard piece of maths work.

clue.text: Recommend a defender

blocks.note: first meaning: to argue in favour of a course
second meaning: a barrister or champion of a cause

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means publicly support, and as a noun it is a lawyer who pleads someone's case.

clue.text: Roads meet in confusion round the North; they can improve things

indicators.note: confusion is disorder, so the letters are jumbled
round means the jumbled letters go around another piece

blocks.note: taken as written
the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A chaotic junction up north where roads come together, and those who fix it.
explanation.definitionFit: Emendators are people who correct or amend texts, making corrections and revisions.

clue.text: Back scores: one known for shooting

indicators.note: back here tells us the letter at the back of the word moves round to the front

blocks.note: tens are scores in a game such as archery

explanation.surface: A shooter's results are reviewed: someone famed for marksmanship.
explanation.walkthrough: The S at the back of TENS goes to the front. The Sten was a British submachine gun of the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sten gun was a cheap British submachine gun, an object famous for firing bullets.

clue.text: The inventor left a little something

blocks.note: Samuel Morse invented the telegraph code
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: The inventor bequeathed a small token.
explanation.definitionFit: A morsel is a small piece or bite, especially of food, a tiny portion.

clue.text: Smooth flow of language, or a mistake?

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: words sliding easily off the speaking organ
second meaning: an accidental error in speech

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is whimsical, reading the phrase literally as speech slipping fluently from the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names an inadvertent spoken error, while its literal reading suggests fluent glib speech.

clue.text: Nitre - active or passive?

indicators.note: active suggests the letters are lively and moving about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A chemistry question: is saltpetre reactive or not?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Active' looks like the opposite of the definition, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Inert means inactive and unreactive, lacking the power to move or act.

clue.text: Empty tray holding rum drink

indicators.note: an emptied word has its inside removed, leaving only its ends
holding means one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: the outside letters
rum means strange, odd

explanation.surface: A bare tray carries a glass of spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the spirit in the drink, but here it is the old British adjective for odd.
explanation.definitionFit: A toddy is a hot alcoholic beverage of spirits, water, sugar and spice.

clue.text: One we get to return in different ways: an attendant

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so these words are read from right to left
in places the turned piece inside the others

blocks.note: a, one
taken as written
two kinds of way: St for street and Rd for road

explanation.surface: We send someone back by various routes to an usher.
explanation.walkthrough: Street and Road are two different ways; their abbreviations go either side.
explanation.definitionFit: A steward is someone who looks after passengers or guests, serving on a ship, plane or at an event.

clue.text: TNT - as in explosive flash

indicators.note: an explosion blows things apart, scattering the letters

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: TNT goes off, as in a sudden explosive flash.
explanation.definitionFit: An instant is a moment, a split second, the same as in a flash.

clue.text: Showing mettle - or metal?

definitions.note: the clue gives the noun; the answer is the adjective, like metal

blocks.note: first meaning: resolute, hard and determined
second meaning: like or made of the alloy of iron

explanation.walkthrough: Mettle and metal sound alike; the word covers both a steely gaze and something literally of steel.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes firm resolve and also a cold grey quality resembling the iron alloy.

clue.text: A group of spectators not right in the cooking area!

indicators.note: not means the following letter is taken out

blocks.note: a gallery is a crowd watching, as at golf
the abbreviation, here removed

explanation.surface: Onlookers crowd into the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A galley is the kitchen on a ship or aircraft, where food is prepared.
